segments.text: Four things your body already knows about water. The tax your heart pays. The two percent line. What too much water does. And the protocol.
Your heart pushes about seven thousand five hundred litres of fluid a day. You only hold five at any moment. Every single beat is that difference.
You are about sixty percent water. In a seventy kilo body that is roughly forty two litres. Two thirds of it sits inside your cells. The rest is the logistics fleet moving heat and fuel.
Here is the number. For every one percent of body weight you lose as water, your heart rate climbs about three beats a minute at the same pace. Same work. More beats.
Now the honest part. Below two percent, in real races, performance mostly holds. That two percent rule came from laboratory protocols. Not from the road. So treat this as a baseline. Not a scare.

Which brings the bigger lie. Eight glasses a day has no scientific basis. It came from one line in a nineteen forty five report that everyone read halfway. And past thirst, in long events, plain water can outrun your sodium. Exercise associated hyponatremia. Since nineteen eighty one it has killed at least fourteen athletes.
Your kidneys filter about one hundred and eighty litres every day and return ninety nine percent of it to you. Thirst is the signal that system sends. It is not a weakness. It is the sensor.

So the protocol. Weigh yourself before and after a hard session. Every kilo lost is a litre. Replace one point two to one point five times that over the next three hours. Keep losses below two percent. That is one point four kilos at seventy.
And a receipt most trainers will not give you. Cramps are not proven to be a salt problem. In ultramarathon runners, sodium did not separate the people who cramped from the people who did not.
Your body already keeps this clock. Twelve breaths a minute. Seven thousand five hundred litres a day. Two percent before it costs you. Read your clock. Then train it.
